articles.title: Passengers in Florida crash identified as family of 4, their caretaker and another couple
articles.summary: The families of the seven passengers who were aboard a Bahamas-bound Learjet that crashed in Palm Beach County, Fla., on Sunday identified their loved ones on social media Monday. “With broken hearts, our families share that Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina were among those lost aboard the flight that went down near Greenacres, Florida, on November 1,” the statement said. Authorities had still not publicly confirmed the identities of those on board the plane at a news conference Monday afternoon, during which they said weather conditions were a major factor in the federal investigation into the fatal crash. The National Transportation Safety Board told reporters on Monday that ice was forming on the jet as it experienced moderate turbulence. Miami air traffic control granted the pilot permission to climb from 35,000 feet to 37,000 feet to avoid precipitation, but shortly afterward, an emergency was declared with a mayday call. Air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC captured the crew's comments leading up to the crash. Someone in the cockpit can be heard saying "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute, Reuters reported. "We're going to crash into the ground," the person said. The Learjet 60, which had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, went down at about 12:50 p.m. ET near Cresthaven, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. The NTSB said all nine people on board were killed, including two crew members and seven passengers. Along with the passengers’ families, Camila Corteleti identified her 20-year-old daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras , as one of the pilots of the private jet that crashed Sunday afternoon, the New York Times reported. The NTSB said it's unclear if Filgueiras was at the controls at the time of the crash. A man who was leaving the area of the crash on Sunday sustained a leg injury, officials said. Dashcam footage posted to social media by an eyewitness showed the aircraft falling toward the ground beside a road and exploding into a fireball, narrowly missing cars and homes. The impact left a "massive crater" near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at a news conference. About 600 residents were evacuated to two shelters, he said. People stand near a crater formed after the Learjet 60 crashed. Vanessa Lara/via REUTERS "We have a lot of work to do on scene — this will be a several-day process," NTSB senior investigator Timothy Monville said during Monday's news conference. "The biggest obstacle we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway." Investigations are also hampered because the crash-site crater is partially filled with water. The NTSB said it will interview witnesses to the accident as part of its investigation and encouraged anyone with relevant information, videos or audio to contact the NTSB by email at witness@ntsb.gov. Some evidence indicates that parts of the plane broke off before the private jet crashed, according to NTSB member Tom Chapman. "I want to note that if any members of the community find debris, please do not move it," he said. "Contact us or local authorities, and we will respond appropriately." He also told reporters that, according to records, a cockpit voice recorder was installed, but the NTSB doesn't know whether it was still on board. "Sometimes these things change over time," Chapman said. "Of course we're very hopeful that we can recover it. Too early to know, but that will be very important data." What we know about the victims Among the victims was the copilot of the private jet, Filgueiras. Her mother said she earned her pilot's license at age 17. The 20-year-old had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and was working for a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, according to her mother. Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras itsnatfilg/Threads It's unclear who the other pilot was or who was at the controls at the time of the crash. According to the Palm Beach Post , the crash killed Helen Sharp, 40, her husband, Adam Robinson, 45, and their two young children. Sharp's father, 70-year-old Dudley Sharp, confirmed the deaths to the outlet. "It's quite a blow," he told the Palm Beach Post. "We had a daughter, her husband and two grandchildren on the plane." Family members of the seven passengers killed in Sunday's crash released a joint statement on Facebook that also identifies the other three passengers: Anita Maria Cetina, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr. "With broken hearts, our families share that Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina were among those lost aboard the flight that went down near Greenacres, Florida, on November 1," the statement said. "Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were the light of their lives.  Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever.  Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives.  Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return." "Charmi and Rachel were full of joy and adventure," the statement continued. "They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building. They are deeply loved, and we will miss them endlessly. Anita Maria cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family.  She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion." The families also thanked first responders, investigators and the Palm Beach community for "their care," as well as "everyone who reached out with love." They added: "Our hearts are also with the families of the pilots, who are grieving alongside us." What we know The aircraft crashed in a residential area in Greenacres. Anadolu via Getty Images The Learjet 60 took off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. FAA records list the owner as a Delaware corporation. The National Weather Service had a flood watch in effect for the area of the crash, Palm Beach County, through Monday afternoon, with rain expected on and off across South Florida. In air traffic control audio posted on LiveATC, someone in the cockpit said they were "managing the ice" but faced "moderate" turbulence and were seeking "better rides." The Associated Press reported the crew also asked to climb. Less than a minute later, the person said "Mayday, mayday," reporting the plane was suddenly descending at 10,000 feet per minute. Seconds later, the person declared an emergency, with the descent rate reaching 20,000 feet per minute. Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: "We're going to crash into the ground," before reporting the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the plane began to bank. Flightradar24 data showed the vertical descent rate at one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute. The last words heard from the cockpit were "we're out of time." The jet is reported to have descended at a peak of 32,000 feet per minute. Anadolu via Getty Images Accuweather reported that thunderstorms in the area produced heavy rainfall and lightning. Driver Aki Kuusisto's dashcam footage captured the moment the jet hit the ground. "I heard a whistling noise, a big bang, and I saw a fireball," he told CBS News . "It felt like it was right next to us... you could feel it in the car." What have other officials said? The FAA said the aircraft departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was heading to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when the crash took place. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis told reporters during a Sunday briefing that there was "a lot of debris" that was strewn over a "pretty significant distance." "It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis said. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road." Transportation Secretary Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy" and said the FAA and Department of Transportation would be investigating the incident. What did eyewitnesses say? Anthony Blackmon, who lives around 500 feet from the site of the crash, told NBC Miami that debris from the crash struck his home. "Debris was everywhere," he said. "Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire. I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today." Adam Itayem told WPTV , "It sounded like a loud boom. I thought it was thunder," adding, "I saw a big crater in the ground and water coming out of the crater and a big fire too." "I heard and felt the boom," Andrew Mannino told CNN , saying he saw a "large black cloud immerse in the air," adding, "The power immediately went out and is still out." Around 600 people were evacuated by Palm Beach County authorities while federal officials investigate the crash. "We're waiting for someone to give us answers about what we're going to do, because they're not even letting us into the community to get our clothes," local resident Jesus Solorzano told WPTV. articles.title: Trump put himself on the midterms ballot without running. Now his legacy is at stake.
articles.summary: President Trump’s political capital is on the line ahead of the midterm elections as a potential blue wave threatens his final two years in office. Trump has crisscrossed the country, holding 28 in-person campaign rallies in addition to a series of tele-rallies. The president has made stops in Republican strongholds like Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and even Alaska in an effort to keep the states firmly in the red column. He’s also visited a number of deep-red states like Mississippi and South Carolina, where polls show closer than expected races. While Trump has argued his rallies have boosted Republican incumbents and candidates in the states, recent polling suggests otherwise. A New York Times/Siena poll released the day before Election Day showed Democrats with leads in Senate races in Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska. Trump’s heavy political investment in the states means he could end up shouldering the blame for a potential blue wave, which could impact the GOP beyond Election Day. Republicans warn that a blue wave would be detrimental to the last two years of the Trump administration, and by extension, his legacy. “It impacts his ability to drive policy over the next two years, or if a Supreme Court nomination comes up, or fill in the blank in terms of even Cabinet turnover,” said one Republican strategist, speaking on condition of anonymity. “All of that too will help shape his legacy, and it’s how people remember you at the end that guides you into the history books.” In a statement to The Hill on Monday, the Republican National Committee (RNC) warned that Democrats would “obstruct” Trump’s agenda and that their “disastrous economic policies” would drive jobs overseas. “The president knows what’s at stake this cycle, which is why he’s barnstormed the country to encourage our voters to support Republican candidates that will advance his agenda and deliver for the American people,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre. But during an election eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump did not appear entirely focused on the elections that could impact the trajectory of his last two years in office. The president spent the first 22 minutes of his 37-minute address — largely viewed as a closing message before the midterms — talking about his administration’s efforts to repair the Reflecting Pool. Trump showed off a number of pre-renovation pictures of the pool and at one point invited Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to the podium to give brief remarks. Trump also touted his numerous beautification projects and lower crime in the nation’s capital. Republican operative Rob Stutzman called Trump’s speech “another Captain Queeg moment,” a reference to a character from Herman Wouk’s 1951 novel “The Caine Mutiny” who is considered an unstable and incompetent commander. A second Republican strategist said, “What the utter f--- was that?” when asked for their reaction to Trump’s speech at the Reflecting Pool. “Republicans were hoping that he would have some sort of a closing message, some sort of American message with it, with a wonderful backdrop that could maybe be of help in the closing hours here,” the unnamed GOP strategist said. “As we Republicans are losing touch with the public, it looked like he was losing touch with reality.” One national Republican operative noted the speech was “not surprising” considering Trump’s communication style but expressed frustration with the closing message. “This perfectly encapsulates his messaging throughout this entire campaign cycle, but it’s deeply frustrating when we need to be laser-focused on turning out our low propensity voters tomorrow,” the operative said. A third Republican strategist defended the speech, arguing the Reflecting Pool was “a hook” for Trump to be able to talk about issues like crime and immigration. “It’s one of these things that wherever you get the opportunity to speak to a national audience, you’re going to talk about the midterms even if you have to start with something else,” the strategist said. Trump did take some time during his speech Monday to urge Republicans to turn out on Election Day. “If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” the president said. “Now, that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is — Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad president — for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms.” “We gave this a very strong shot,” he added. Much of the GOP’s strategy has hinged on turning out its low-propensity base as much as possible, arguably a tall order for any political party in a nonpresidential election. Republicans hoped to defy that trend by dispatching Trump on the campaign trail, urging voters to “pretend” like he is on the ballot. “The amount of rallies he did shows he ‘believes’ that he’s on the ballot tomorrow,” said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor. “He worked hard, and he’s right: Tomorrow’s outcome is a reflection on him.” In a statement to The Hill, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle referred to Trump as the GOP’s “best messenger” and “unmatched motivator” who is “committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.” But some Republicans are unsure whether that tactic will ultimately work. “So far from what we’ve seen, those rallies have not done what they were meant to do,” said the first unnamed Republican strategist. Democrats have been heartened by signs of early turnout in key battlegrounds, but Republicans argue that a large share of their voters tend to vote in person on Election Day. “They’re banking on these Republicans and the folks that he’s trying to rally to show up tomorrow, and Republicans historically and should do exceedingly well tomorrow,” the first Republican strategist said. “But the fact is, they still underperformed in places like Texas and in Florida in the early vote.” According to data released by Texas’s secretary of State, 7.7 million voters in the Lone Star State voted early. Meanwhile in Florida, registered Republicans led registered Democrats in early voting by just a little more than 200,000 voters. By comparison, in 2022, registered Republicans led Democrats in early voting by just a little less than 500,000 voters. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Sunday sounded the alarm over low turnout in the state, which has become known as a nerve center for Republican politics. “If people stay home, you could end up seeing results that you’re going to be wondering what happened. That’s just the reality,” DeSantis said at a campaign event. “The reality is gas is higher, and that’s not good. Some of these Republicans act like it’s no big deal. I disagree with that. It is a big deal to people,” the Florida governor continued. Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media, Inc. All rights reserved. This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. articles.title: Prosecutors announce intention to retry Lindsay Clancy for deaths of her 3 children
articles.summary: Prosecutors announced in court on Nov. 2 that they intend to retry Lindsay Clancy , the Massachusetts mother who killed her three young children. Clancy, 36, was charged with murder for killing her children Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, on Jan. 24, 2023, by strangling them with exercise bands in the basement of their Duxbury home. Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington argued she can't be held criminally responsible, Massachusetts' version of the insanity defense, because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. Clancy's triple murder trial ended with a hung jury in early September, leaving her fate in limbo. Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague said prosecutors want to retry Clancy but are waiting to decide what charges she will face until Judge William Sullivan makes a decision on three motions, including a defense motion to dismiss the murder charges. "Your honor, this would be a retrial. As to what that looks like will depend," Sprague said. "We're not at that point yet." Reddington argued prosecutors don't need to know the outcome of the motions to determine what charges they will retry Clancy on. "Why do we not know if the next trial will be murder in the first degree, or a lesser charge or no charge?" he asked. Reddington said he wants Sullivan, who is approaching mandatory retirement in June, to preside over the trial in the spring. Sullivan said requested the parties appear on Nov. 16 for another hearing. If Sullivan dismisses the defense's motion to dismiss at that hearing, the parties will then select a trial date, which Sullivan said he is hoping to schedule in March. Judge to weigh motion to dismiss The defense team pushed to have the charges against Clancy dismissed altogether and launch an investigation into the holdout juror. Defense attorney Martin Weinberg argued on Nov. 2 that retrying Clancy would violate constitutional protections against double jeopardy because Sullivan should have questioned the jury more thoroughly after receiving notes indicating one juror was refusing to follow the court's instruction on reasonable doubt, an allegation the holdout juror has denied . Sullivan interjected, noting he did question the jurors individually before declaring a mistrial on Sept. 4. Weinberg said the question Sullivan asked was “simply constitutionally insufficient to probe what was going on in that jury room." Prosecutors opposed the defense's motion , saying the mistrial was properly declared after the jury repeatedly reported it was deadlocked. Sprague argued that Sullivan could not have questioned the jurors further without probing the substance of deliberations, which is prohibited, and even if he could have done so, the appropriate response wouldn’t be dismissing the charges. "It’s not for the trial judge to choose sides in a deadlocked jury and decide," she said. Sullivan said he would take the matter under advisement. Defense argues for holdout juror probe Reddington also requested the holdout juror's phone, phone records and confidential questionnaire, among other records. Reddington asked the court to question the juror about the truthfulness of a questionnaire and his answers during jury selection, a "sworn assurance" from Sept. 3, and the use of a cell phone or receipt of outside information during deliberations. In a fiery exchange on Nov. 2, Reddington said he has evidence the holdout juror was using his cellphone and researching altruistic filicide during deliberations. Reddington said the juror was also dishonest about his criminal history on his questionnaire. Heather O'Connor, an attorney for the holdout juror, said that the mistrial decision had to be made based on what was known at the time and that these allegations came to light after the jury was dismissed. "And to be clear Juror Doe does not concede any of those allegations," O'Connor said. Sullivan said he would take the matter under advisement. Prosecutors push for gag order Prosecutors also asked the court to prohibit defense attorneys, as well as themselves, from speaking to the media in a way that would "have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceedings." Sprague argued Reddington has already made many statements that were inappropriate and "calculated to affect the public's perception of the case," including asking for a presidential pardon and saying the other jurors were "robbed" by the holdout. A defense attorney opposed that motion, arguing that such an order would constitute "prior restraint" of speech that infringes upon both Reddington's and Clancy's First Amendment rights. They said that no trial date had been set and the impact of these alleged comments on a potential future jury is "merely speculative." Sullivan said he would also take this matter under advisement. articles.title: Elon Musk is tightening Grok limits as the cost of AI catches up with demand
articles.summary: Elon Musk said on Sunday that Grok ( SPCX ) users would run up against usage limits more quickly than normal because servicing Grok Bot has become too expensive. "The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on his social media platform, X. The sudden throttling highlights one of the biggest questions swirling around the AI revolution: whether demand from users will be enough to sustain a business. It turns out, at least in Musk's case, that demand isn't the problem. The cost is. Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent. User demand is just one side of the AI market equation, and the businesses churning out sophisticated and expensive models have to — or will have to, eventually — generate revenue to cover their heightened costs. The economics of the still-new and messy AI industry suggest that even healthy demand can't always sustain the AI tools they're selling. Not at these prices — for the users (cheap) and for the corporate compute (expensive; just look at the computing bills ). That's why the revenue question is increasingly critical and why Musk's admission is so significant. The AI business is running into real-world limitations. Musk suddenly changing Grok subscriptions so that the AI-usage meter runs faster has struck users and tech observers as unfair and worrisome for SpaceX's business. Elon Musk arrives to speak at an indoor Presidential Inauguration parade event in Washington, Jan. 20, 2025. (AP Photo/Matt Rourke, File) AP Photo/Matt Rourke "Two weeks ago Grok Bot was an incredible success story powering SpaceXai's revenue growth. Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X .  Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance." The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull." Musk, as he does, is posting through it. "Just being sensible," he wrote on X , in response to a comment suggesting that investors would punish SpaceX for the decision. In fact, shares are up 5% on Monday. And why shouldn't they be? Wall Street has always loved fiscal responsibility and capitalizing on demand. Another way to think through the change is that Musk was simply offering an introductory rate to hook users. Perhaps AI subscriptions are going through their own version of the "VC subsidy," popularized when Uber, Lyft, and other venture-backed apps offered discounts and super-low rates to boost adoption and engagement, only for the apps to sharply increase prices once users became reliant on the services. The classic introductory rate strategy. Grok, a user might ask, is that true? Follow Hamza Shaban on X @hshaban . articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump admin's bid to set aside thousands of California ballots
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s push to force California to set aside thousands of ballots from people the federal government claims are noncitizens, a decision that came hours before the final day of voting in the pivotal midterm elections . The high court refused to immediately intervene in a case involving 20,000 people the Republican administration flagged as likely noncitizens on the largely Democratic state’s voter rolls. The swift rejection capped a string of losses for the president’s effort to intervene in the election before the counting of ballots to decide who controls Congress in the last two years of his second term. No justices publicly dissented. “The Court rejected Trump’s emergency request without even asking the other side to respond,” California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, posted on X. “Democracy won.” Several lower courts also rejected the Justice Department's push to set aside the challenged California ballots until the voters’ citizenship status could be verified. And in a case that revolved around the future certification of Alaska's election results, a judge did not even hold a hearing before dismissing a Trump-ordered suit to prevent a possible Democratic Senate win. The high court did not detail its reasoning in the California ballot case, as is common in emergency decisions. The justices previously rejected Trump’s push to restrict mail ballots around the country in September, even though the justices have sided with his administration in a series of other emergency docket appeals. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, also a Democrat, noted the administration's legal losing streak in a statement. “Courts have now rejected the Trump Administration’s attempts to interfere in California’s elections not once, not twice, not three times, but four times — from the district court to the Ninth Circuit to the U.S. Supreme Court,” Bonta said. “This latest decision should put an end to the Administration’s attempt to disrupt California’s elections through emergency court orders." Voting by noncitizens is rare in the US The Republican administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite it being a rare problem . California officials said the administration's list appeared to be filled with errors and said setting the ballots aside could effectively disenfranchise legal voters. Also on Monday in Washington, another federal judge ruled against the administration’s efforts to make last-minute demands of California election officials, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution. “The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution’s Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone,” Chief Judge James Boasberg wrote. Later Monday, ruling in a separate case, Boasberg declined to issue yet another order against the administration to cease the demands. He ruled that Democratic groups that sued did not have legal standing and that the issue already had been dealt with by states and the courts. The administration, for its part, said segregating the ballots was a modest request that would eventually allow legal votes to still be counted. Its push has faced not only the remarkable series of losses in court, but criticism for waiting until a few weeks before the election to make its demands of California election officials with a list that even the Department of Justice admits is not entirely reliable. During a hearing over whether to lift her order forbidding the administration from threatening to prosecute election workers who let potentially illegal voters cast ballots, U.S. District Court Judge Trina Thompson drilled down on reports of widespread inaccuracies in the Justice Department's data. “Would you agree there's a high error rate?” the San Francisco-based judge asked Kenneth Kao, a Justice Department attorney. “That's a fair statement,” Kao said. “That's why we ask for the registrars' aid in verifying these are all valid voters.” At the same time, Bill Essayli, the federal prosecutor running the Justice Department's Los Angeles office, said at a news conference he was highly confident the people on the list were not entitled to vote. “This isn’t speculation. This isn’t a theory,” Essayli said, later conceding there may be errors on the list. Californians have already been casting ballots for weeks Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. Each of the state’s roughly 23 million registered voters is mailed a ballot, and more than 6 million have already been returned, according to Associated Press elections data. “The DOJ’s baseless challenge was yet another attempt at federal overreach and voter suppression,” Kristen Clarke, the NAACP's general counsel, said in a statement in reaction to the Supreme Court decision. "We will not stand for the Trump Administration’s bullying campaign, and we will continue to use every tool at our disposal to ensure the American people’s voices are not silenced.” California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible. Lower courts swiftly sided with the state, with a district judge warning last week that segregating ballots would “wreak havoc” on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process. “If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat. A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California’s unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the “violation of federal law.” ___ Associated Press writers Sophie Austin in Sacramento, California, and Safiyah Riddle in Los Angeles contributed to this report. ___ Follow the AP's coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court . articles.title: Which party has a better chance of winning the midterms? What the final polls say.
articles.summary: The 2026 midterm elections are tomorrow. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data. The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. And they have been wrong before . Yet time is almost up — and the stakes on Nov. 3 couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too. The state-by-state midterm landscape has reached its final form — and the polling trends are clear. Here are the numbers on the eve of Election Day. The generic congressional ballot Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds). You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading. History is helpful here, courtesy of the RealClear Politics polling average : At this point in 2022 — after nearly two years of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (2.5 percentage points) on the generic ballot. On Election Day, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House. At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.3 points on the generic ballot. The next day, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But by the eve of Election Day, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 8.7 points and 63 seats, respectively. So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — nearly 9 percentage points , on average. And that margin has held steady over the last month. Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House. Advantage? Democrats. 12 specific Senate races National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow: Maine (Republican seat) Republican Susan Collins (incumbent) Democrat Troy Jackson What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena University poll shows Jackson ahead by 6 . Michigan (Democratic seat) Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress) Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director) What the latest polls say : Eighteen polls were conducted in October. Seventeen of them showed El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 1 to 9 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena University survey gives El-Sayed an 11-point lead ; new polls from YouGov ( El-Sayed +4 ) and Research Co. ( El-Sayed +2 ) show smaller margins for the Democrat. Ohio (Republican seat) Republican Jon Husted (incumbent) Democrat Sherrod Brown (former senator) What the latest polls say : Brown has edged Husted in nearly every poll conducted since the first week of October, with margins ranging from 2 to 6 percentage points. The final New York Times/Siena University survey gives Brown a 6-point advantage . Georgia (Democratic seat) Democrat Jon Ossoff (incumbent) Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with October polls putting him ahead by an average of 9 percentage points . A new Echelon Insights survey gives Ossoff a 15-point lead . North Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman) Democrat Roy Cooper (former governor) What the latest polls say : Cooper leads by nearly 11 points, on average . Final polls from YouGov and East Carolina University show him ahead by 11 points and 9 points, respectively. New Hampshire (Democratic seat) Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator) Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative) What the latest polls say : Pappas and Sununu were previously trading leads in polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7.5 percentage points — over the last month. The final University of New Hampshire survey shows him ahead by 12 . Alaska (Republican seat) Republican Dan Sullivan (incumbent) Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress) What the latest polls say : Surveys conducted in October show Peltola leading by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena Universty poll gives her a narrow 48-46% advantage . Iowa (Republican seat) Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress) Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete) What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries . The final YouGov and New York Times/Siena University polls show Turek ahead by 1 point; GrayHouse and co/efficient polls show Hinson leading by 2. Texas (Republican seat) Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general) Democrat James Talarico (state legislator) What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted this fall has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins were small — between 2 and 6 points. But the Democrat seems to be closing strong: final polls from Atlas Intel and the New York Times/Siena University show him ahead by 6 and 7 points, respectively. Nebraska (Republican seat) Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor) Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support) What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent nonpartisan results suggest Osborn could be competitive, and a couple of Osborn-affiliated polls show Ricketts and his independent challenger trading small leads. An Echelon Insights poll released on Tuesday shows Ricketts ahead by 1 point; a New York Times/Siena University survey released on Saturday gives Ricketts a 6-point lead. Kansas (Republican seat) Republican Roger Marshall (incumbent) Democrat Adam Hamilton (Methodist pastor who previously considered an independent run) What the latest polls say :  Only one survey conducted over the last month shows Marshall ahead (by a single point). The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). A new CNN poll has Hamilton up by 4 ; a new Emerson College survey puts him ahead by roughly the same amount . On Friday, the Washington Post released a poll showing Hamilton lapping Marshall by about 10 points. But the paper questioned its own results , noting that Republicans responded at much lower rates than Democrats. The final New York Times/Siena University survey shows Hamilton ahead by 5 . South Carolina (Republican seat) Republican Darline Graham (incumbent, appointed to replace her brother Lindsey Graham after his death in July) Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrician and former U.S. House candidate) What the latest polls say : Graham held a narrow lead in most fall surveys . But it was small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well. A partisan poll released on Friday gave Andrews a 5-point advantage; a new New York Times/Siena University poll shows the two candidates essentially tied. Advantage? Democrats. They've been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong. Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability President Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., on Oct. 20. KENT NISHIMURA via Getty Images To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle. At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 59.4% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 38% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -21.5% — near his all-time low. Here's a sampling of Trump's latest net approval numbers from a few top pollsters: New York Times/Siena University : -26% American Research Group : -38% CNN/SSRS : -35% Reuters/Ipsos : -35% Again, history can provide perspective . In late-October 2018, Trump was about 10 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November. According to the New York Times , Trump has the second lowest approval rating heading into the midterms since 1946, behind only Harry Truman. George W. Bush's approval rating was higher at this point in 2006 — a year in which Democrats went on to flip the House and Senate. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 70% disapprove and 25% approve. That's a 45-point gap. In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency  — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection. Advantage? Democrats. articles.title: Haley Stevens' Democratic allies turn on her after surprise GOP endorsement
articles.summary: Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Michigan, speaks alongside Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers after a church service at Perfecting Church, in Detroit on Sunday, November 1, 2026. - Jose Juarez/AP As recently as Saturday night, the prospect of Democrat Haley Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race had seemed implausible. Stevens issued a statement praising Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed for saying he disagreed with a controversial advertisement that blamed the high cost of living in Michigan on the United States’ aid to Israel. Despite a week of speculation about her withdrawing an endorsement for El-Sayed, her primary rival, she repeatedly said that she would do no such thing. When staffers reached out last week to urge her not to endorse Rogers, Stevens replied in a text message, according to a person who saw the message: “Omg why would you think I would do that??!!” At midnight Saturday, she told a key ally that she was sticking with El-Sayed. Then on Sunday morning, things changed. She appeared at a Black church in Detroit with Rogers and then announced her change of heart to reporters gathered outside and on social media. Her move stunned the political world — including Stevens’ friends, colleagues and even her own congressional staffers, most of whom found out about her decision on social media and promptly quit, according to a statement from her chief of staff and people familiar with the matter. The question that could decide Michigan’s Senate race — and potentially, with it, which party will have majority control of the chamber for the last two years of Donald Trump’s presidency — is whether Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers will change votes or amount to more than political melodrama. There have long been signs of discontent with El-Sayed within the Democratic coalition. Stevens was strongest in the August primary with Black and Jewish Democrats, some of whom have balked at supporting El-Sayed, a Muslim who is a strident critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza and an advocate for ending foreign aid for Israel’s military. Prior to Stevens’ defection, CNN’s most recent poll of the Michigan Senate race had El-Sayed leading Rogers by seven points – with 95% support from Democratic likely voters. Already, Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers is becoming something of a rally-around-the-flag moment for Democratic leaders — uniting a coalition in the race’s final days around a shared sense of the stakes at hand. Among the Democratic leaders who denounced Stevens and strongly backed El-Sayed were two of his most powerful intra-party critics: Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who tacitly supported Stevens in the primary, and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who just days ago said El-Sayed’s views on Israel were “wrong” and “more than concerning.” Schumer accused Stevens of a “despicable betrayal.” “Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” the New York Democrat said . Schumer added that Democrats “are equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans.” Pelosi, meanwhile, said on social media that El-Sayed “must win,” and that Stevens “has chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers.” As Stevens and Rogers spoke to reporters outside the church after the service, an individual in the crowd shouted: “Haley’s a traitor!” An El-Sayed campaign spokesperson said he raised $2.4 million on Sunday after Stevens endorsed Rogers — marking his “biggest fundraising day yet.” What Stevens said on CNN In an interview Sunday night with CNN’s Anderson Cooper, Stevens said that endorsing Rogers was “just a weight off my shoulders.” But she struggled to answer questions about why she’d changed her mind. “Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier,” Stevens said. “There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in, or this is a campaign you don’t belong in.’” What she didn’t explain, despite being asked several times, was what had changed between Saturday — when she told several Democrats she intended to appear with El-Sayed and Clyburn at church — and Sunday morning, when she instead went to a Detroit church with Rogers and endorsed him. She said she was tired of watching El-Sayed stand with Hasan Piker — but didn’t address the reality that El-Sayed’s campaign appearances with Piker came before the primary election, and Stevens had endorsed El-Sayed after that primary’s conclusion. “I’m just sick of the people he stands with,” Stevens said. Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Democrat who had told CNN Sunday that Stevens reassured her Saturday that she wasn’t switching sides, reacted by saying: “That was one of the most painful interviews I have ever watched.” Why did Stevens switch her endorsement? Shortly after their primary, which El-Sayed won by less than a percentage point, the two hugged at a state party unity breakfast. But they had not campaigned together in months – or spoken directly during that time, as CNN reported last week. Democrats attempted to negotiate a joint appearance Sunday at a Black church in Detroit alongside South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the party’s most influential figures. The goal was to shore up Black support for El-Sayed. One longtime Michigan Democratic operative said many older Black voters tend to cast their ballots on Election Day, rather than voting early, “because of a well-earned higher skepticism of absentee voting.” Those votes could be an essential piece of the Democratic coalition El-Sayed is trying to hold together. Stevens said in a statement Friday morning that Clyburn, who endorsed and campaigned with her in the primary, had invited her to the church — and that she would be attending, marking the first time she would appear jointly with El-Sayed on the campaign trail. However, she also issued a list of demands for El-Sayed — including attempting to pressure him into denouncing an outside group’s new advertisement that blamed the United States’ foreign aid for Israel for Americans’ struggles with high costs. The ad features two people in a grocery store suggesting they can’t afford basic goods due to the aid. It echoed what El-Sayed has often said on the campaign trail about Israel, even as he distanced himself from the ad. El-Sayed responded in a statement Friday night that Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” It became clear that the joint appearance wouldn’t happen late Friday, when CNN and other outlets reported that El-Sayed’s campaign had asked Stevens to skip all campaign events in the race’s closing days. Dingell said on CNN Saturday that she was the one who delivered the message to Stevens. Still, on Saturday, El-Sayed denounced the ad, and Stevens issued a statement praising him for doing so — developments that made her decision Sunday more of a head-scratcher to many Democrats close to her. Dingell told CNN Sunday that Stevens had reassured her overnight that she wasn’t switching sides. Standing next to Rogers on Sunday, Stevens mentioned four times that El-Sayed’s campaign had excluded her from his events. She pointed to it again in her endorsement video posted on X, noting El-Sayed “had said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he’s right.” “My vote for Senate is going to be with Mike Rogers, and I will tell you why. Because we have to stand with country. We can’t stand with hate. We can’t stand with Hasan Piker,” she said. Party officials moved swiftly on Sunday to publicly condemn Stevens and criticize her focus on being uninvited. But they privately said there was blame to go around — notably for El-Sayed. “He acted like he won the primary in a landslide, but he didn’t,” one longtime Democratic official told CNN. “Abdul gave himself his own October surprise.” El-Sayed went ahead Sunday with the event. After asking reporters to focus on questions about issues facing people in his state rather than “two folks who aren’t here right now,” El-Sayed was asked if he believed Stevens had betrayed his party by backing Rogers. “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, standing next to Clyburn. “I think about, like I said, the 9,999,998 people who are not those two. Because you know what? I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.” Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed attends a church service at Greater Emmanuel Institutional Church of God in Christ, Sunday, November 1, 2026, in Detroit. - Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP A core tension in Michigan reemerges A deeply emotional argument for many in the Democratic Party became particularly personal for El-Sayed and Stevens, both of whom are known for not listening much to advisers and following their own instincts. Stevens was backed in the primary by tens of millions of dollars in spending from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a flashpoint between her and El-Sayed, who denounced AIPAC and the influence of money in politics at nearly every campaign event. El-Sayed was criticized for campaigning with Piker, the stridently pro-Palestinian live-streamer with a long history of controversial comments about Jews, including comparing Jewish residents who oppose El-Sayed to members of the Ku Klux Klan, remarks widely denounced as antisemitic. AIPAC on X reshared Stevens’ video on Sunday endorsing Rogers. During the primary, El-Sayed portrayed Stevens as an AIPAC puppet and called her “the least capable candidate in America.” “Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” Stevens responded on X days before the August 4 election . As AIPAC’s allied groups boosted her campaign, the animosity grew too. El-Sayed’s multiple shots at Stevens as being a puppet angered her and made her dig in. Meanwhile, she was rankled by his repeated refusal to affirm that Israel had a right to exist as a Jewish state and his statements that it was committing genocide in Gaza and that funding to the country was hurting Michiganders. Many of Stevens’ Democratic critics on Sunday blamed Stevens’ fiancé, Michigan lawyer Jason Turkish, who endorsed Rogers last week and did media interviews criticizing El-Sayed as uncommitted to Jewish safety. One former Stevens staffer noted Sunday that after she and Turkish became engaged in May — something they kept private until after the August primary — Stevens grew more focused on defending Israel and AIPAC, even as the Democratic Party and US public opinion as a whole has become more skeptical of Israel. In the ex-staffer’s view, she was speaking less about the message she’d run on and won with before: growing Michigan’s economy and protecting manufacturing. The topic often came up while preparing for interviews or donor calls, the staffer said. Preparing for a June interview, Stevens pressed aides on why she should avoid defending AIPAC when she had done so in a 2022 House primary against former Rep. Andy Levin and won. Speculation about Turkish’s influence burst into the open on Sunday, as Democrats — many of whom had either spoken to Stevens recently or been briefed by people who had — suggested he was playing an outsized role for a candidate’s partner. Former Pennsylvania Rep. Susan Wild, who in 2023 was Stevens’ roommate in Washington and whose children regularly text with Stevens, said she was “terribly sad and disappointed” by her friend’s “appalling” move. “If this is because of her new relationship (about which many of us were so happy for her after she lost the primary), all I can say is that any woman who abandons her friends when a new guy comes along is no friend at all,” Wild said. Stevens’ mother, Maria Marcotte, a retired advertising executive, told CNN in a statement that her daughter’s fiancé had nothing to do with the change of heart — and that Marcotte herself had also voted for Rogers. “Haley is her own woman. She always has been. Suggesting a man made her decision for her is insulting to her, and it is insulting to me as her mother,” Marcotte said. She pointed to episodes in which progressive pro-Palestinian activists hounded Stevens during the primary campaign. “Abdul should not have thrown her out of the campaign for speaking her truth,” she said. “Haley made this choice herself, with her eyes open, the way she has made every hard choice in her life. And I know Haley will support whoever wins this election, because that is who she is. I have never been prouder of her.” Who’s to blame? The anger between the two rivals kept growing from a distance after El-Sayed won the primary. El-Sayed grouped Stevens in with all those he decided he didn’t need to build his coalition after his primary victory. Stevens would tell people that she thought he was running a weird and losing campaign, but that she didn’t feel it was her obligation to fix it. Rogers aides, aware that his path to victory largely depended on a Democratic civil war, restrained themselves to spreading word of discontent and convincing themselves they weren’t just fantasizing that they could get her all the way to endorsing. Then came the grocery-store ad that rekindled the tension. It was released by a group linked to Cenk Uygur, co-creator of The Young Turks and — in a twist practically designed to create acrimony — Piker’s uncle. As Stevens demanded he denounce Uygur’s ad, El-Sayed returned to name-checking AIPAC in his statement criticizing Stevens, something Michigan attorney general Dana Nessel, a Stevens primary backer who has raised concerns about Jewish safety, asked him to stop doing before she endorsed him. Nessel told CNN in October that El-Sayed had agreed to her request. Stevens’ defection threatened to worsen El-Sayed’s standing with Jewish voters. Rogers has already predicted publicly that he could win as much as half the Jewish vote on Tuesday. “It feels like over the last eight weeks, Dr. El-Sayed has become more egregious in the language he’s been using,” said Rabbi Aaron Starr, the president of the Michigan Board of Rabbis and a leader of the “Nonnegotiable” group of Jewish leaders. That group calls on El-Sayed to do more about concerns regarding Jewish safety and to affirm Jewish sovereignty in Israel. Starr and other Jewish leaders held a call Sunday afternoon to discuss the endorsement flip. But Stevens was also damaged with key allies. Dingell, long a peacemaker within the state party, chided Stevens’ “continued efforts to get attention.” “Unfortunately, she’s seriously hurt herself,” Dingell told CNN. Curtis Hertel, the chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party, effectively booted Stevens from it. He wrote on social media: “Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.” Many Democrats in the state felt that for most of the preceding year, Stevens was viable in the Senate race largely because she’d cornered Schumer into effectively backing her. Into the spring, complaints circulated about what a lackluster primary campaign she was running, how much she was struggling on the stump, and how she was lashing out against those who wouldn’t support her. Despite her eventual strength with African American voters, Black church leaders were angry about her efforts to push for early endorsements. Chokwe Pitchford, a 27-year-old district commissioner from Benton Harbor and seen as a local rising star, told a story that he says encapsulated the kind of experience other Michigan Democrats he knows had: One morning, he discovered a graphic online from Stevens saying he’d endorsed her, even though as he posted in response, they’d never spoken. “Instead of reaching out and apologizing, I had people from around the state calling from unknown numbers saying my political career is over if I don’t take that down,” Pitchford told CNN. “Some of us tried to ring this alarm bell a year ago; there was a problem here.” Indeed, the most robust praise for Stevens on Sunday was coming from Republicans. “Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. The story and headline have been updated with additional information. Todd reported from Detroit. CNN’s Dana Bash, Manu Raju, Nicky Robertson and Jeff Zeleny contributed to this report. articles.title: Man completes 31,000-mile walk around the world and returns to mom’s house
articles.summary: HULL, England (AP) — Karl Bushby embraced his weeping mother in his arms Monday as he returned to his northern England home to complete a 28-year odyssey to walk around the world . “Where have you been?” his mother, Angela, asked as he arrived outside the home he left in 1998 that was now decked with a banner saying “Welcome Home Son.” He didn’t need to tell her. Bushby set out from Punta Arenas, Chile, on Nov. 1, 1998, and walked 31,000 miles (50,000 kilometers) across four continents and 30 countries to get home. He navigated shifting ice over the Bering Strait and swam across the Caspian Sea and English Channel to avoid taking a boat or plane — or any transport — to propel him forward. He vowed not to return until he could complete the journey on foot. It was an eye-opening adventure full of danger and drudgery that was interrupted for years at a time by the unexpected: the 2008 financial crash that sapped funding from sponsors, the 2020 COVID-19 pandemic and mountains of bureaucratic red tape to get across international borders. A trek made possible by kind strangers On the final day of the journey, Bushby pushed his cart toward a hero’s welcome at City Hall before setting off for the last stretch to see his mother. “Sorry to keep you waiting,” he joked to the crowd of hundreds who cheered his arrival. “Is that it, is it done?” The ex-paratrooper said he looked like he was 10 years old when he left his mother's row house at the age of 29. He returned at 57 — softer, grayer and weathered, but far more worldly. “They say it takes a village but literally it took a world to get me here,” Bushby said. “The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation states to get me back here today. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth.” The idea started with a birthday card from his dad Bushby had a thirst for adventure, but his mission only came into focus when his father, Keith, sent him a birthday card in the mid-90s. His dad, an army veteran himself, mentioned an argument two special forces troops had about the possibility of walking from London to New York over the Bering land bridge, believed by some scientists to have been used by early humans to migrate from Asia to the Americas at a time of lower sea levels. Perilous jungles, scorching deserts and frozen tundra slowed him down, but bureaucratic holdups brought his adventure to a halt for long periods. Bushby originally calculated the distance could be covered in about five years, but he knew that was unrealistic. “You just dump a whole bucket full of reality on that,” he said. “We suspected that it was 12 years plus. And the plus was a big plus. But never in our wildest dreams would we ever have imagined 28 years.” Danger on land and sea followed by border problems He dodged Colombia's armed conflict in the dangerous Darién Gap, the roadless and rugged jungle, rainforest and mountains between South and Central America in 2001, and was then jailed for 18 days after crossing a restricted border zone in Panama. After being airlifted to safety during the 56-mile (90-kilometer) Bering Strait crossing in 2006 with American adventurer Dimitry Kieffer, they started again and faced a standoff with a polar bear, survived near-death plunges into freezing waters and almost lost all their supplies when their sleds plunged in the sea. After managing the rare crossing, the pair were jailed and faced deportation for entering Russia illegally. It took Bushby almost 10 years to make his way through Russia in fits and starts because of visa struggles and weather that only allowed travel a few months a year. When Russia denied him a visa in 2012, Bushby walked in protest from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., which eventually led to him getting the proper paperwork. Family firsts and a long-awaited reunion Bushby has met several times over the decades with family members who have met up with him on his journey. He was greeted on the beach in Dover by his father and brothers after crossing the channel last month. He reunited with Adam, his 36-year-old son from an early marriage whom he had rarely seen, and he met his 12-year-old granddaughter for the first time, which he said was amazing. Bushby hadn't seen his mother in a decade, setting the stage for an emotional and somewhat awkward reunion captured amid a throng of cameras and a documentary film crew. “Behave yourself, mother,” he joked, as his mother wrapped her arms around him and wept. “Get yourself together.” He said he had long tried to imagine that moment he would return to find his mother at the gate where he left her so long ago. He said it was an emotional reunion that was “one great, big, blurry mess” he was trying to process. “It was kind of almost shocking to see my mother after so long,” he said at a news conference later. “She’s changed a lot. We’ve all changed a lot in that time.” Next steps for a man who walked millions In the final days of his trip, Bushby spoke of his anxiety over the trip ending, not knowing what he would do next and coming to terms with having to live in his mom’s basement. “It’s like stepping across the event horizon into a black hole,” he told The Associated Press. “I have no idea what’s about to happen in my life.” There will be plenty to keep him busy. Six speaking engagements are scheduled in the next two months, a sequel to his memoir “Giant Steps" is due and German filmmaker Werner Herzog is making a documentary on his trek. He expects to struggle with the ups and downs other adventurers have experienced after long journeys. “The only way I think, you know, you get over that is just get another mission, another passion and get busy,” he said. “That’s what I intend on doing.” ___ Melley reported from London. articles.title: U.S. strikes Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on eve of midterms
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, a U.S. official said Monday, on the eve of crucial midterm elections . Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. The official, who wasn’t authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that “Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets” had been targeted. The strikes appeared to be limited as opposed to a return to full hostilities but followed President Donald Trump previously saying the U.S. would not launch new strikes on Iran before Tuesday's midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress. The region is on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes, which were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal, are certain to raise fresh concerns. Backchannel negotiations also are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than 8-month-old war that’s rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran. The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September , but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers hauling Iranian oil from getting to the global market. Plus, a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are on their way to the Middle East. Before the strikes were confirmed, U.S. Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal could still be struck. Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, but the White House has offered scant details. Trump told reporters that letter was focused on assisting Iran with “medical supplies and various things.” “We’ve had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” Vance told reporters Monday when asked about the letter. “I actually just spoke with the president of the United States about an hour ago about this. Look, the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We’re going to keep on working at it.” Netanyahu pushed Trump for strikes in a weekend call Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections , according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu to form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week's elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials. The two officials said the mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports. They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials. One official said Netanyahu was working with senior officials in the U.S. administration to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign and that the president does not appear to have made a decision. Netanyahu pressed for strikes during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it. Other U.S. allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying that would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved . The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trump’s discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call. Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said he spoke by phone Monday with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth about “the latest regional and international developments” and the Houthis’ continued attacks on Saudi Arabia. Trump downplays scale of Iran conflict Oil prices dropped sharply Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts in the Iran war appeared to show signs of headway. Trump noted the drop in a speech in Washington on Monday, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion. “I don’t know if you even call it a war, because we haven’t been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said. Iran says it is prepared for war while pursuing diplomacy Iran wants guarantees that the U.S. will implement its side of any agreement. The U.S. and Israel have twice attacked Iran while it was engaged in negotiations over its disputed nuclear program. Iranian officials say publicly they are prepared for war or diplomacy. The new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei , met with Iran’s military chiefs and said the response to “any kind and level of threat” from the U.S. or Israel should be immediate and without “geographic limits,” urging an expansion of the list of potential targets. A recent analysis by The Associated Press found that Iranian strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases since the start of the war have caused billions of dollars in equipment damage. Rezaei, the Iranian security chief, told state television that “the tone has completely changed” from the U.S. and called it a “very good sign.” He gave no details about the letter from Vance and said he had not responded. Arab allies are caught in the middle October saw the most attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since March, as Iran has tried to ramp up economic pressure on the U.S. to get it to lift its blockade. The mood was grim at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies. United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash told attendees the U.S. and Iranian stances are far apart, and “if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.” Gulf nations have spent billions of dollars to boost their defense capabilities since the war began. Egypt’s Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty told the gathering in Bahrain that the next escalation “will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere.” China will send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters Monday. ___ Magdy reported from New York, and Anna from Jerusalem. Victoria Eastwood in Cairo, Kanis Leung in Hong Kong and Katie Marie Davies in London contributed to this report. ___ AP STANDARDS: The AP uses anonymous sources only when the information is vital to the news report and not opinion or speculation. The information must be unavailable except under the conditions of anonymity imposed by the source. The source must be reliable, in a position to have accurate information and approved by news managers. articles.title: Savannah Guthrie makes new plea about missing mother after finding daughter's drawing
articles.summary: "TODAY" co-host Savannah Guthrie issued a new plea for information about her missing mother, Nancy Guthrie, on Sunday, nine months after the 84-year-old was abducted from her Tucson, Arizona, home. Guthrie shared an old drawing made by her daughter, Vale, showing a blue umbrella in the rain and the words, "I know it might not seem like it, but I really need my mommy." "Found this old drawing from my daughter today," Guthrie wrote on Instagram. "It says so much about how I feel." "The world goes on, things appear ‘normal’ — as we try to keep going and be strong, especially for our young kids — but it’s not and it never will be," she continued. Savannah Guthrie Urges Public To Help Find Missing Mother Nancy In Emotional Mother’s Day Post "For Annie and Tommy, for Cam and Kristine, for Mike and me and for all of Mom’s beloved grandchildren: We ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward," Guthrie wrote. Read On The Fox News App "We need someone to help us, tell us what you know. Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves. The reward is still available. Please. We are begging you. Please help us." Guthrie also thanked those who have supported her family and urged people to "join us in praying without ceasing." Three Months After Nancy Guthrie's Abduction, Sheriff's Office Renews Plea As Key Questions Remain Unanswered Nancy Guthrie was reported missing Feb. 1 after she was last seen at her home in the Catalina Foothills area near Tucson shortly before 10 p.m. Jan. 31. Authorities believe she was taken against her will. A masked, armed individual was captured on the home's doorbell camera footage, apparently tampering with the device. The FBI and Pima County Sheriff’s Department have not identified a suspect, and no arrests have been made. Savannah Guthrie Was 'Surprised And Dismayed' By Doubts She Would Return To 'Today' After Mom's Disappearance The home of Nancy Guthrie, the missing mother of "TODAY" show host Savannah Guthrie, is seen from above, Thursday, Feb. 5, 2026, in Tucson, Ariz. Guthrie has continued to push for answers about her mother’s disappearance while returning to work on "TODAY." During a June appearance on "TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle," she rejected the idea that she had forgotten about her mother. "I know maybe people wonder, ‘What’s going on? How is she able to do that job? Is she not thinking about it? Did she forget?’ No. Never," Guthrie said. "It’s always with me. I cry every morning on the way to work, and I cry every morning on the way home," she added. Savannah Guthrie Delivers 'Very Specific' Message To Mom's Kidnapper 25 Weeks After Her Abduction In August, six months after her mother's disappearance , Guthrie and her siblings also issued a statement asking for information about their mother. "Every day, we wake up and try to be strong and go on — because that’s what our joyful and resilient Mom taught us to do. But make no mistake — our hearts are in ruins," Guthrie wrote. "Cam and Kristine, Annie and Tommy, Mike and me — we spend every waking moment thinking of her, longing for her, looking for her." The Pima County Sheriff’s Department said Friday the Nancy Guthrie Task Force was continuing to work with laboratories to advance DNA analysis. "Earlier this month, investigators traveled to Florida to meet with lab scientists to see what more could be done to advance this case," the department wrote on X. "A number of ideas were discussed, and we continue to work with all our partners to solve this case." The agency reminded the public that no tip is too small. Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos previously said Guthrie "did not leave on her own." Nancy Guthrie Ransom Demands Released By Pima County Sheriff's Department In Bid To Identify Sender A supportive sign left by neighbors is posted outside the home of Nancy Guthrie, the 84-year-old mother of television host Savannah Guthrie, who went missing from her home in Tucson, Arizona, U.S. February 4, 2026. Authorities released the contents of two ransom notes in July. The first, sent Feb. 2, claimed Guthrie was safe and demanded $4 million in bitcoin for her release. The second, sent four days later, claimed she had died shortly after being kidnapped. Investigators said the notes contained distinctive writing patterns and asked anyone who recognized the style to contact authorities. A possible additional ransom text message reported in September was later deemed not credible by investigators.
